cse-2017-1-cs-40.approach: Belady’s anomaly cannot occur for stack algorithms (LRU, OPT); random replacement is not a stack algorithm and can make FIFO-like choices.

steps.title: S2 (LRU)
steps.body: LRU is a stack algorithm: the pages in memory with k frames are always a subset of those with k+1 frames, so faults never increase with more frames. S2 is false.

steps.title: S1 (random)
steps.body: Random replacement can pick exactly the victims FIFO would pick, so on the classic FIFO anomaly string it can fault more with 4 frames than with 3. S1 is true.

answer.value: S1 is true, S2 is false

cse-2017-1-cs-41.approach: Following the official key, each query restricts t through EMP: t’s EmpName must come from an EMP tuple u, so the result is bounded by EMP’s finite contents, and every quantifier ranges over a finite relation (EMP or DEPT).

steps.title: What "safe" asks
steps.body: A TRC query is safe if it always returns a finite result whose values come from the database (its domain).

steps.title: All three queries
steps.body: In (I), (II), (III) the outer part $\exists u\in EMP(t[EmpName]=u[EmpName]\wedge\dots)$ ties $t$ to an EMP tuple, and the inner quantifier ranges over the finite relation DEPT — (I) keeps employees whose DeptId matches no department (e.g. NULL), (II) those whose DeptId differs from some department, (III) those whose DeptId matches one. The official key treats all three as safe.

(II) is equally bounded through u ∈ EMP.
(I) is accepted as safe: it reads as employees with a NULL / unmatched DeptId.
All three are safe according to the official key.

cse-2017-1-cs-42.approach: Identify the scheme: if the requester T2 is older (smaller timestamp), it kills (wounds) the holder T1; a younger requester waits. This is wound-wait.

steps.title: Deadlock-free
steps.body: A transaction only ever waits for an *older* one (T2 waits only when TS(T2) > TS(T1)). Waits follow strictly decreasing timestamps, so no wait-for cycle can form.

steps.title: Starvation-free
steps.body: A killed transaction restarts with its original timestamp, so it keeps aging; eventually it is the oldest, is never killed again, and only waits for transactions that terminate.

optionAnalysis.reason: Wound-wait with original timestamps on restart.
Keeping the timestamp prevents starvation.
Waits only go from younger to older — no cycle.
It is both deadlock-free and starvation-free.

cse-2017-1-cs-42.verification: Matches the standard wound-wait properties (and the official key A).

Assuming nested ifs — the then/else parts are expressions, not statements.

cse-2017-1-cs-45.approach: One stop-and-wait cycle = frame transmission + propagation + processing at receiver + ACK transmission + propagation + processing at sender. Efficiency = time spent sending useful (non-overhead) bits ÷ cycle time.
cse-2017-1-cs-45.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Bit rate | $1$ Mbps |
| Propagation delay | $0.75$ ms |
| Processing time per frame | $0.25$ ms |
| Information frame | $1980$ B (of which $20$ B overhead) |
| ACK frame | $20$ B |

steps.title: One complete cycle
steps.body:
Frame goes out, propagates, is processed; the ACK goes back, propagates, is processed:

$$T_{cycle} = 15.84 + 0.75 + 0.25 + 0.16 + 0.75 + 0.25 = 18.00\text{ ms}$$

scene.caption: ACK arrives and is processed at $t = 18$ ms; the next frame can start.

steps.title: Efficiency
steps.body:
$$\eta = \frac{T_{data}}{T_{cycle}} = \frac{15.68}{18.00} = 0.8711 \Rightarrow 87.11\%$$

The official key accepts the range **86.5 to 89.5**, because slightly different conventions are in use: counting processing only once gives $\frac{15.68}{17.75} = 88.34\%$, and counting the whole frame as useful gives $\frac{15.84}{18} = 88.00\%$. All of these fall inside the range.

pitfalls: Forgetting the ACK transmission time ($0.16$ ms) or the return propagation delay.
Using the full $1980$ B as useful data while the question explicitly lists $20$ B of overhead.
Using only one-way propagation delay in the cycle.
cse-2017-1-cs-45.verification: Recomputed the cycle by components: transmissions $15.84 + 0.16 = 16$ ms, propagation $2 \times 0.75 = 1.5$ ms, processing $2 \times 0.25 = 0.5$ ms, total $18$ ms.

cse-2017-1-cs-48.approach: Binary search for the first 1; each probe is a yes/no comparison, so an information-theoretic bound with 31 positions (plus the "no 1" case) gives $\lceil \log_2 32 \rceil = 5$, which binary search attains.

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.body: The answer can be any of the 31 indices (or "no 1 at all") — up to $32$ outcomes. Each probe returns 0 or 1, so $k$ probes distinguish at most $2^k$ outcomes. $2^4 = 16 < 31$, so 4 probes are not enough; we need $k \ge 5$.

steps.title: Binary search attains it
steps.body: Probe the middle; if it is 1 the boundary is at or left of it, else to its right. The candidate range shrinks $32 \to 16 \to 8 \to 4 \to 2 \to 1$, i.e. exactly $5$ probes in the worst case.

scene.caption: First probe at the middle index 15 halves the 32 possibilities.

pitfalls: Answering 31 (linear scan) — not optimal.
Using $\lfloor \log_2 31 \rfloor = 4$; the ceiling is required.

cse-2017-1-cs-49.approach: PC-relative: $\text{target} = (\text{address of next instruction}) + \text{Offset}$. Measure the byte distance from instruction $i+4$ back to instruction $i$.

steps.title: Addresses
steps.body: Let instruction $i$ be at address $A$. Each instruction is 4 bytes, so beq ($i+3$) is at $A + 12$ and the next instruction ($i+4$) is at $A + 16$.

steps.title: Offset
steps.body: $$\text{Offset} = \text{target} - \text{PC}_{next} = A - (A + 16) = -16$$

pitfalls: Measuring from the branch itself (gives $-12$).
Giving the offset in instructions ($-4$) instead of bytes.
cse-2017-1-cs-49.verification: Going back 16 bytes from $A+16$ skips exactly 4 instructions ($i+3, i+2, i+1, i$) and lands on $i$. ✓

cse-2017-1-cs-50.approach: Pipeline clock = slowest stage + buffer delay. Time for $n$ instructions on a $k$-stage pipeline is $(k + n - 1) \times$ clock. Compute for both pipelines and divide.
pitfalls: Forgetting the 2 ns buffer delay in the clock period.
Keeping 5 stages for EP — splitting OF makes it 6 stages, adding one fill cycle.
Taking the clock of EP as 10 ns (EX) — OF1 at 12 ns is now the slowest.
cse-2017-1-cs-50.verification: Steady-state check: ratio of clocks $22/14 = 1.571$; the extra fill cycle of EP lowers it to $1.51$, consistent.

cse-2017-1-cs-51.approach: 256 blocks / 2 ways = 128 sets, so blocks 0, 128, 256 share set 0 and 1, 129, 257 share set 1. Simulate LRU on one set for the first pass and a later pass; the other set behaves identically.

steps.title: Map blocks to sets
steps.body: Sets $= 256/2 = 128$. Set $= \text{block} \bmod 128$: $0, 128, 256 \to$ set 0; $1, 129, 257 \to$ set 1. The two halves of the sequence are independent and symmetric.

steps.title: Pass 1 on set 0
steps.body:
0 M, 128 M, 256 M (evict 0), 128 H, 0 M (evict 256), 128 H, 256 M (evict 0), 128 H.

Misses: 3 compulsory (first touch of 0, 128, 256) + **2 conflict**.

scene.caption: Pass 1: 3 compulsory + 2 conflict misses in set 0.

steps.title: Every later pass on set 0
steps.body:
The set starts as $\{128, 256\}$ with 128 most recent. 0 M (evict 256), 128 H, 256 M (evict 0), 128 H, 0 M, 128 H, 256 M, 128 H.

Block 128 never leaves; 0 and 256 keep evicting each other: **4 conflict misses** per pass.

scene.caption: Pass 2 (and every later pass): 4 conflict misses.

steps.title: Total
steps.body:
Set 0: $2 + 9 \times 4 = 38$ conflict misses. Set 1 is identical: $38$.

$$\text{Total} = 38 + 38 = 76$$

pitfalls: Counting the first-time misses of 0, 128, 256 (and 1, 129, 257) as conflict misses.
Forgetting set 1 (doubling).
Using FIFO instead of LRU — 128 stays resident only because it is re-used every other access.

cse-2017-1-cs-52.approach: Draw the expression tree and use Sethi–Ullman-style ordering: evaluate the deeper right subtree first with 2 registers, then the left. Constants are immediates, so they need no register.

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.body: The final `mul` needs both of its operands in registers at the same time, and arithmetic cannot read memory, so at least $2$ registers are needed.

steps.title: Code with 2 registers
steps.body:
Evaluate the larger subtree $((b+c)/3)+d$ first:

```
LOAD R1, b
LOAD R2, c
ADD  R1, R1, R2   ; b+c
DIV  R1, R1, #3   ; (b+c)/3
LOAD R2, d
ADD  R1, R1, R2   ; ((b+c)/3)+d
LOAD R2, a
SUB  R2, R2, #1   ; a-1
MUL  R1, R2, R1   ; result
```

No spill, only R1 and R2 used.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Lower bound 2 is achieved, so $X = 2$.

pitfalls: Loading constants 1 and 3 into registers — immediates are allowed.
Evaluating $(a-1)$ first, which holds a register while the right subtree needs two more (3 total).
cse-2017-1-cs-52.verification: Sethi–Ullman labels: leaves $b$ (left) $=1$, $c=1$ ⇒ $b+c = 2$; $/3$ keeps 2; $+d$ keeps 2; $a-1 = 1$; root $= \max(1, 2) = 2$.

cse-2017-1-cs-53.approach: Both `strlen` results are `size_t` (unsigned), so their difference is computed in unsigned arithmetic and wraps around instead of going negative.

steps.title: Evaluate the condition
steps.body:
`strlen(s) = 3`, `strlen(t) = 5`. As unsigned 32-bit values:

$$3 - 5 \equiv 2^{32} - 2 = 4294967294$$

Compared with `c = 0` (unsigned): $4294967294 > 0$ is **true**.

steps.title: Pick the branch

cse-2017-1-cs-54.approach: The address splits as TAG | INDEX | OFFSET. Going from direct-mapped to 16-way keeps the offset and total width but cuts the number of sets by 16, moving $\log_2 16 = 4$ bits from INDEX to TAG.

steps.title: Direct mapped
steps.body: Lines $= N/B$, index bits $= \log_2(N/B)$, offset bits $= \log_2 B$, TAG $= 10$.

steps.title: 16-way set associative
steps.body:
Sets $= \dfrac{N}{16B}$, so index bits $= \log_2(N/B) - 4$. The address width is unchanged, so

$$\text{TAG} = 10 + 4 = 14\text{ bits}$$

pitfalls: Subtracting 4 instead of adding — fewer sets means fewer index bits and more tag bits.
Using 16 instead of $\log_2 16 = 4$.
cse-2017-1-cs-54.verification: Fully associative limit: all index bits move into the tag; 16-way moves 4 of them.
